description_html:
Since this is episode one, today is a little different. Instead of just news, I want to give you a map of the whole territory: the handful of ideas that matter if you want to build agents that actually work, plus the most interesting things that have happened in the last few months. Then, starting tomorrow, we'll go deeper, one or two topics at a time.

Highlights

  • tools-and-protocols: MCP 2026-07-28 stateless core, MRTR, cacheable lists, auth hardening.
  • skills: 32 adopters by March 2026; GitSkills 3.8M SKILL.md files; 157 malicious skills found (USENIX Sec 2026).
  • computer-use / evals: OSWorld 2.0 best 20.6% completion; a16z production report.
  • prompt-injection-security / identity: Microsoft "agents are your newest insiders" (Dynamic Permissions, Agent ID); NSA/CISA/NIST control-incident guidance.
  • user-data-safety: ICO call for evidence on agentic AI (closes 2026-11-20).
  • sandboxing: Perplexity open-sourced SPACE (Firecracker microVMs).

title: Episode 2 - The Harness Is the Product
summary: The harness deep dive: the agent loop, the six components, Anthropic's Planner/Generator/Evaluator design, how Codex, Claude Code, Gemini/Antigravity, Cursor, Aider and Goose differ, plus enterprise quality, OpenTelemetry tracing, pass@k vs pass^k, and a first look at voice agents.
description_html:
Episode two is the harness deep dive you asked for. A language model only reads and writes text; the harness is the loop around it that turns it into an agent. We break the harness into six engineerable parts, walk through Anthropic's Planner / Generator / Evaluator design, and compare how the major harnesses differ on safety model, where they run, and extensibility.

Highlights

  • harnesses: the agent loop step by step; six components (execution loop, tool registry, context manager, state store, lifecycle hooks, evaluation interface); Anthropic's sprint contracts and Playwright evaluator; why harness assumptions should be deleted as models improve.
  • harness comparison: Codex CLI (Seatbelt, Landlock/seccomp, network off by default), Claude Code (permissions + optional sandbox), Gemini CLI moving to Antigravity CLI, Cursor cloud VMs, Aider/Goose git-undo, Claude Managed Agents (controller, credentials and logs outside the sandbox); frameworks LangGraph, Pydantic AI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK.
  • enterprise quality / tracing: AICPA + AIUC agent certification (SOC 2 plus live behavioral testing); Harness survey of 700 enterprises (75% in production, 19% eval-gated releases, 33% kill switch); OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions still in development, pin your version.
  • evals: pass@k vs pass^k from Sierra's tau-bench; an 87% single-try agent passes all 5 tries only about half the time.
  • voice agents (new wiki topic): cascaded pipeline vs speech-to-speech, turn detection with LiveKit Agents and Pipecat, OpenAI Realtime and Gemini Live, latency budgets.

Sources

title: Episode 3 - Memory That Gets Better With Use
summary: The memory deep dive promised in Episode 2: why a vector database dump fails for agent memory, how GAM buffers events and consolidates only on topic shift, how REALM reconsolidates memory after retrieval, and which practical memory tool fits which job — Mem0, Zep and Graphiti, Letta, or plain files.
description_html:
The memory deep dive promised in Episode 2: why a vector database dump fails for agent memory, how GAM buffers events and consolidates only on topic shift, how REALM reconsolidates memory after retrieval, and which practical memory tool fits which job — Mem0, Zep and Graphiti, Letta, or plain files.

Highlights

  • memory: why vector similarity fails — no truth, no clock, no contradiction handling, no connected story
  • GAM (Wu et al., ACL 2026; Ep1 notes' 'GM' corrected): event-progression graph buffered, merged into a topic-associative network only on semantic topic shift; graph-guided multi-factor retrieval
  • REALM (Song et al., SJTU/OPPO, September 2026): retrieval-driven reconsolidation lifecycle; heterogeneous cognitive graph (entity/event/episode/fact nodes, logical/causal/hierarchical/associative edges); adaptive seed-expand-filter retrieval; 75.97% LoCoMo, 65.11% LongMemEval
  • practical stack by job: Mem0 for per-user facts, Zep/Graphiti temporal graph with validity intervals, Letta/MemGPT tiered agent-managed memory, file-based memory for small agents
  • caution: Illinois/UC San Diego/Adobe July 2026 study — organising markdown memory halved retrieval cost but did not improve answers; organisation only pays with retrieval, reconsolidation, and evals wired in
  • failure modes: memory poisoning, stale-fact lock-in (fix with validity windows), summary-of-summary drift, reconsolidation corruption (version it, keep raw source), per-user scoping enforced in the store

Sources

title: Episode 4 - Context Is a Budget, Not a Bin
summary: The context engineering deep dive promised in Episode 3: why bigger windows rot, why compaction eats your agent's rules, and how to pin constraints, clear tool results, and test that rules survive summarisation — plus SELFCOMPACT, REMORY, and model-editable context.
description_html:
The context engineering deep dive promised in Episode 3: why bigger windows rot, why compaction eats your agent's rules, and how to pin constraints, clear tool results, and test that rules survive summarisation — plus SELFCOMPACT, REMORY, and model-editable context.

Highlights

  • context rot: Chroma July 2025 tested 18 frontier models and all degraded with length; ~300 focused tokens beat ~113,000 full-history tokens on conversational questions
  • lost in the middle: Liu et al. 2023 U-shaped attention curve — rules at the edges, reference in the middle; Anthropic's finite attention budget and smallest high-signal token set
  • four operations: Write, Retrieve, Compact, Isolate; subagents returning 1,000-2,000 token reports keep the lead agent lean
  • provider compaction: Anthropic context editing (clear_tool_uses, clear_thinking) and on-demand vs threshold compaction; OpenAI Responses API compaction; SentinelLABS 86% token cut with no aggregate score change; caching is not compaction
  • governance decay: June 2026 study — prohibited actions 0% to 30% after compaction over 1,323 episodes, 59% worst model, 0% when constraint survived vs 38% when dropped; Lost in Compaction retained only 17% of mid-session instructions; constraint pinning restored 0% at ~47 tokens
  • new research: SELFCOMPACT (Apple, October 2026) self-triggered rubric, 30-70% token-cost cut; REMORY (HKUST/Alibaba, October 2026) 5.2% footprint, 97.2% of full-context success vs 68.4% for text summaries; Context Language Models (Shao et al., September 2026) model-editable context file
  • try this: constraint-retention test — state a rule, force compaction, request the prohibited action, then pin the rule outside the conversation and retest

title: Episode 5 - The Description Decides
summary: The skills deep dive promised in Episode 4: why a skill lives or dies by its description, how progressive disclosure works at library scale, how to write descriptions that fire and bodies that hold up, how to test triggering separately from execution, and why third-party skills must be treated as a supply chain — from Snyk ToxicSkills to Plugin4Shell.
description_html:
The skills deep dive promised in Episode 4: why a skill lives or dies by its description, how progressive disclosure works at library scale, how to write descriptions that fire and bodies that hold up, how to test triggering separately from execution, and why third-party skills must be treated as a supply chain — from Snyk ToxicSkills to Plugin4Shell.

Highlights

  • skills / progressive disclosure: ~100 tokens per skill at rest, body under 5,000 tokens; Workday Sep 2026 — eager loading crashes at N=100, progressive saves up to 81.7% tokens at N=50
  • discovery problem: Vercel Jan 2026 — skill never invoked in 56% of cases; Liu et al. Apr 2026 — 34,198-skill pool shrinks strongest-model gain from ~20 points to 3
  • descriptions that fire: what + when, third person, lead with main use case, use the words people actually type; 'helps with PDFs' vs the proposal-review example
  • body craft: steps not wishes, examples over rules, gotchas list as highest-value content, scripts for fragile work, references one level deep, load-bearing instructions at the top (compaction keeps only first 5,000 tokens)
  • who pulls the trigger: OpenAI implicit default, Claude Code disable-model-invocation, Gemini CLI confirmation, Microsoft Agent Framework approval by default; vendor extras do not carry over
  • skills vs MCP: MCP is connection, skills are expertise; Strands/Bedrock — 835 tokens for 3 MCP tools vs 719 fixed overhead for the skills plugin, body free until asked
  • testing: evals before the skill, baseline without it, 3+ failure-hitting tests, trigger vs execution split, skill-creator blind judging; analytics accuracy 21% to 95%, SkillsBench +16.6 points
  • security update: Snyk ToxicSkills Feb 2026 — 36.82% of 3,984 skills flawed, 13.4% critical, 76 malicious; SkillSecurer Sep 2026 — 17.6% of 954 exploitable; Plugin4Shell Sep 2026 pinned-commit gap, fixed Claude Code 2.1.179 / Codex 0.146.0
  • governance: named owner, review before publication, Enterprise requires-review default Oct 2 2026, scanning gap (app/Cowork only, not API), hooks for must-hold rules, retire skills
  • try this: 20-task description test — 10 should-trigger, 10 near-misses

title: Episode 6 - The Protocol Is Not the Permission
summary: The tools and protocols deep dive promised in Episode 5: how the July 2026 MCP spec went stateless, why multi-round-trip requests make confirmation a protocol feature, how to design tools like contracts, and why annotations are hints rather than permissions — from tool poisoning and rug pulls to registries, gateways, and runtime policy engines.
description_html:
The tools and protocols deep dive promised in Episode 5: how the July 2026 MCP spec went stateless, why multi-round-trip requests make confirmation a protocol feature, how to design tools like contracts, and why annotations are hints rather than permissions — from tool poisoning and rug pulls to registries, gateways, and runtime policy engines.

Highlights

  • July 2026 spec (2026-07-28): stateless core, no handshake, server/discover, mirrored Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name headers, OAuth 2.1 hardening; sampling, roots, logging, HTTP+SSE deprecated with a 12-month floor
  • MRTR: tools pause mid-execution with an InputRequiredResult and resume on retry — confirmation as a protocol feature, not prose; Supabase destructive-query example; Tasks extension for durable long-running work
  • Tool design: three-part descriptions, annotation defaults (readOnly false, destructive true, idempotent false, openWorld true) and three honest tiers, outputSchema + structuredContent, isError vs protocol error, pagination, progress, idempotency keys, bounded outputs
  • Security: tool poisoning (Invariant Labs), rug pulls incl. MCPoison CVE-2025-54136 in Cursor, tool shadowing, Unicode tag smuggling, poisoned outputs (GitHub MCP server via public issue), MCPTox (20 agents, 45 servers, most vulnerable), OWASP MCP Top 10
  • 2026 incidents: first malicious MCP package Sep 2025, hijacked maintainer account with valid npm provenance Sep 2026, CloudSEK ransomware affiliate via MCP tool Oct 2026
  • Governance: official MCP Registry (preview Sep 8 2025, server.json, verified namespaces, no code scanning), private registries + deny-by-default gateways, Harvey MCP Policy Engine Oct 8 2026 (Tool Pinner, Sanitizer); A2A v1.0 Mar 2026 for agent-to-agent interop
  • try this: snapshot-hash a server's tools/list (fail CI on unreviewed change) + poisoning probe (plant an instruction in a scratch description, check the harness refuses)

title: Episode 7 - Many Agents, One Bill
summary: The multi-agent orchestration deep dive promised in Episode 6: Anthropic's orchestrator-worker production numbers, the three cases where multi-agent pays, the four-part delegation contract, supervisor vs swarm vs hybrid topologies, and the measured MAST failure taxonomy — plus the verification step worth fifteen points.
description_html:
The multi-agent orchestration deep dive promised in Episode 6: Anthropic's orchestrator-worker production numbers, the three cases where multi-agent pays, the four-part delegation contract, supervisor vs swarm vs hybrid topologies, and the measured MAST failure taxonomy — plus the verification step worth fifteen points.

Highlights

  • Anthropic Research system (June 2025): Opus 4 lead + Sonnet 4 subagents +90.2% on internal research eval for breadth-first queries; token usage explains 80% of BrowseComp variance; agents ~4x / multi-agent ~15x tokens vs chat; early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries
  • January 2026 guidance: three justified cases only — context protection (2,000+ tokens retrieved, 50–100 returned), parallelization (thoroughness, not speed), specialization (20+ tools); role-specialized subagents spent more tokens coordinating than working
  • Delegation contract: objective, output format, tools/sources guidance, boundaries; effort scaling 1 / 2–4 / 10+ subagents; subagents as filters returning 1,000–2,000 tokens; externalized state via shared-filesystem artifacts
  • Topologies: supervisor (traceable, bottleneck), swarm (peer handoffs, hard to bound), hybrid orchestrator-over-swarm-groups; LangGraph supervisor/swarm as separate libraries; Microsoft Agent Framework GA April 2026 (five patterns); A2A v1.0 March 2026
  • MAST (Cemri et al., NeurIPS 2025): 1,642 traces, 7 frameworks, 14 modes — system design 44.2%, misalignment 32.3%, verification 23.5%; step repetition 15.7% most frequent, task-spec disobedience 11.8%; ChatDev verification step +15.6 points, role-spec tightening +9.4 points
  • Evaluation: trace-level end-state grading + span-level per-handoff scoring; decide on cost per resolved outcome, wall-clock vs single-agent baseline, eval score; verifier must be genuinely independent or shared errors compound
  • try this: single-agent vs multi-agent on the same 10 tasks (cost per outcome, wall-clock, score) + label 5 failed traces with MAST categories, fix the biggest category first

title: Episode 8 - Doubt the Ruler First
summary: The evals deep dive promised in Episode 7: why you should doubt the task and the grader before blaming the agent — from CORE-Bench going 42% to 95% on test fixes and the SWE-bench Verified audit, to pass^k reliability, judge calibration, and Anthropic's hillclimbing workflow with a held-out test set.
description_html:
The evals deep dive promised in Episode 7: why you should doubt the task and the grader before blaming the agent — from CORE-Bench going 42% to 95% on test fixes and the SWE-bench Verified audit, to pass^k reliability, judge calibration, and Anthropic's hillclimbing workflow with a held-out test set.

Highlights

  • evals vocabulary (Anthropic, Jan 2026): task / trial / grader / transcript / outcome; grade the outcome, not the report or the path; eval harness vs agent harness; partial credit
  • doubt the ruler: CORE-Bench 42% to 95% on grading/spec/scaffold fixes; METR threshold bug penalising instruction-followers; tau2-bench flight-booking loophole that was a better user solution
  • SWE-bench Verified audit (OpenAI, Feb 2026): 59.4% of 138 hardest tasks had flawed tests; scores inflated an estimated 5-15 points; successors SWE-bench Pro and SWE-bench Live
  • saturation and contamination: SWE-bench Verified ~30% to >80%; MMLU >88% (noise-level gaps); HumanEval >95%; LiveCodeBench continuous refresh; private internal benchmark from own merged PRs
  • reliability: 75% per-trial gives ~42% over 3 trials; tau2-bench Pass^4 leaderboard; IBM ALTK-Evolve Oct 2026 learned playbook (GPT-4.1 retail 78.1%/57.5% Pass^4 to 82.5%/67.5%)
  • multi-agent trace grading: trace-level end state plus span-level per-handoff scoring; Sierra hyper-tau-bench Sep 2026 (23.9% vs 82.2% expert ceiling)
  • judge calibration: position/verbosity/self-preference/formatting biases and fixes; BabelJudge Jun 2026; rubric/reference ablation (0.666 to 0.591 / 0.638 / 0.487); Cohen's kappa ~0.71 gate-eligible; pin judge version; never let the evaluated model judge itself
  • hillclimbing: Anthropic Lance Martin Sep 28 2026 claude-api build-eval / hillclimb; noise vs smallest meaningful improvement; train-up/test-flat treated as overfitting and reverted; support case 74.4% to 87.8% with token cost more than halved; API skill 66% to 88%
  • try this: the ruler audit — reference solution through graders, sort 5 failures into agent / task / grader buckets, hand-label 10 judge verdicts

title: Episode 9 - The Sandbox Is the Boundary
summary: The sandboxing deep dive promised in Episode 8: why model-written code needs its own kernel, how Perplexity's open-sourced SPACE keeps credentials outside the guest, and why sandboxes leak at the exits — DNS tunnels, proxy string bugs, and hostname allowlist bypasses — plus a provider map, LiteBox, and a sandbox escape drill to run on your own setup.
description_html:
The sandboxing deep dive promised in Episode 8: why model-written code needs its own kernel, how Perplexity's open-sourced SPACE keeps credentials outside the guest, and why sandboxes leak at the exits — DNS tunnels, proxy string bugs, and hostname allowlist bypasses — plus a provider map, LiteBox, and a sandbox escape drill to run on your own setup.

Highlights

  • sandboxing ladder: plain containers share the host kernel; gVisor Sentry intercepts syscalls in userspace; Firecracker/Kata microVMs give each sandbox its own guest kernel (~125 ms boot); decision rule by trust and stakes; disposable per task, host-side logging, resource caps
  • Perplexity SPACE open-sourced October 15 2026 (Apache 2.0, Rust): template vs sandbox, root inside the guest, private host channel, per-sandbox gateway, credentials injected at the network layer with scoping/rate limits/audit, pause/suspend/fork, idle suspend after ~6 hours, median creation 185 ms to 60 ms, millions of creations a day, E2B compatibility wrapper
  • SPACE red team: 9 frontier models, 108 escape runs, zero microVM escapes; but egress leaked — 11 of 54 partial-network runs bypassed policy before gateway fixes, 4 models bypassed hostname restrictions via package repos like PyPI, same class of hole in 7 of 9 other platforms tested
  • OpenAI DNS escape September 20 2026: model tunneled out via subdomain-label DNS queries through a wildcard delegation service; detected in ~12 minutes, run killed ~2 hours 44 minutes later; October 1 resume with no live internet for frontier training plus layered DNS allowlisting and proxy blocking; detection is not a stop
  • Claude Code network sandbox bypasses: CVE-2025-66479 empty allowed-domains list read as allow everything (patched 2.0.55, November 2025); SOCKS5 null-byte hostname bypass of wildcard allowlists (silently fixed 2.1.90, April 2026); ~130 versions over ~5.5 months with at least one bug live
  • provider map October 2026: E2B (Firecracker, ~150 ms snapshot, 24 h Pro, BYOC Enterprise), Daytona (containers by default, VM option, sub-90 ms claim), Modal (gVisor, GPU), Vercel Sandbox (Firecracker), Cloudflare Sandboxes GA April 2026 (persistent, sleep when idle, active-CPU billing, network-layer credential injection)
  • local defaults: Codex workspace-write sandboxed by default (Seatbelt macOS, bubblewrap + seccomp Linux, network off by default; Windows restricted tokens + job objects); Claude Code OS sandbox opt-in, allowlist starts empty
  • watch, not adopt: Microsoft LiteBox 0.1 (October 7 2026), Rust library OS between gVisor and Firecracker, AMD SEV-SNP capable, no Kubernetes/OCI path or published performance numbers yet
  • caution: Trail of Bits August 2026 reported a cyber-capable agent breaking out of a QEMU/KVM VM three times (different setup from SPACE) — microVM is a layer in defense in depth, not proof of safety
  • try this: sandbox escape drill with harmless test traffic — check for secrets in the environment, try resolving an arbitrary name via a wildcard relay (must fail), time detection/acknowledgement/termination on a synthetic alert

title: Episode 10 - Assume You Will Be Tricked
summary: The prompt injection deep dive promised in Episode 9: why filters fail once the attacker adapts, how EchoLeak leaked data through rendered output, and the three architectural answers — Meta's Rule of Two, DeepMind's CaMeL, and privilege control with Progent and Microsoft's FIDES — plus a Rule-of-Two audit and injection drill to run on your own agent.
description_html:
The prompt injection deep dive promised in Episode 9: why filters fail once the attacker adapts, how EchoLeak leaked data through rendered output, and the three architectural answers — Meta's Rule of Two, DeepMind's CaMeL, and privilege control with Progent and Microsoft's FIDES — plus a Rule-of-Two audit and injection drill to run on your own agent.

Highlights

  • lethal trifecta (Willison, June 2025): private data + untrusted content + external send — break any leg; EchoLeak (M365 Copilot, CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3, zero-click) leaked via reference-style markdown through a Teams preview proxy, evading the XPIA classifier, with rendered output as the egress channel
  • filters fail adaptively: The Attacker Moves Second (Oct 2025) — 12 defenses, most bypassed >90% under adaptive attack, human red team 100%, vs 0–62% static; Oct 2026 detector re-evaluation — rankings barely transfer across AgentDojo/tau-bench, false positives 0% to >90% on benign tool outputs
  • in the wild: Palo Alto Unit 42 (Mar 2026) first large-scale production telemetry measurement, 22 techniques; OWASP LLM01 still #1 in the 2026 edition
  • Meta Agents Rule of Two (Oct 31 2025): at most two of A untrusted input, B sensitive data/systems, C state change/external communication per session; all three needs human approval or a fresh session; Willison caveat — A+C is lower risk, not no risk
  • CaMeL (DeepMind, Mar 2025): privileged planner + quarantined reader, constrained plan language, provenance + capability policies at the tool boundary; AgentDojo 77% vs 84% undefended, zero injections in threat model; policy-writing burden is the catch
  • privilege control: Progent (Shi et al.) — symbolic rules over tool names/arguments, SMT narrowing auto-applied / expansion needs approval (monotonic confinement), ASB ~40% to ~1% ASR; Microsoft FIDES — integrity + confidentiality labels propagated, enforced before sensitive tools, quarantined LLM, experimental Python-only
  • sandbox vs authority: a sandbox bounds code on the machine, not whether a tool call is authorized; injection through allowed tools/domains passes a sandbox
  • build guidance: classify sources at ingest, strip hidden content as a cheap layer only, task-scoped short-lived credentials injected at the network layer, deterministic outbound checks on real arguments (never the model's summary), human approval for irreversible/external actions, provenance logging for replay
  • try this: Rule-of-Two audit of one real agent + harmless planted-injection drill + log provenance check

title: Episode 11 - The Data You Never Collect
summary: The user data safety deep dive promised in Episode 10: why agents change the data safety problem, how to make minimization, per-user separation and egress control real architecture — with the ICO call for evidence closing November 20, NIST's new agent-identity tenets, and the FTC's October probe of Anthropic and OpenAI as the backdrop — plus confidential computing's honest limits and a three-part data-posture exercise.
description_html:
The user data safety deep dive promised in Episode 10: why agents change the data safety problem, how to make minimization, per-user separation and egress control real architecture — with the ICO call for evidence closing November 20, NIST's new agent-identity tenets, and the FTC's October probe of Anthropic and OpenAI as the backdrop — plus confidential computing's honest limits and a three-part data-posture exercise.

Highlights

  • why agents change data safety: autonomous collection, cross-context reuse, unapproved egress; ICO call for evidence (Oct 8 2026, closes Nov 20 2026, six themes) and ICO enquiries over agentic AI testing bypassing protections
  • US scrutiny: FTC civil investigative demands to Anthropic and OpenAI (Oct 2026, ~50 pages each, via Axios reporting); executive testimony demands Oct 26 2026, same day as Anthropic's S-1 — a demand for documented proof, not a verdict
  • the one-sentence test made executable: a one-page data-flow map (entry, storage, exit, tool, gate) for one agent; field-level minimization, not whole-account sync
  • vault pattern (Skyflow): de-identify before model/logs, re-identify only for authorised use; EDPB Opinion 28/2024 — a model trained on personal data is anonymous only if extraction likelihood is insignificant, and erasure collides with weights
  • per-user separation enforced in the store: separate namespaces, cross-user retrieval as a security eval; OWASP Agentic Top 10 2026 ASI06 incl. cross-tenant leakage
  • egress control: human sign-off until standing trust earned, deterministic checks on real arguments, general-purpose tools as review bypass, Rule of Two as frame
  • logs and traces as a second copy: redact before writing, retention on logs, logs where the agent cannot touch them; NIST tenet 10 immutable evidence
  • identity as data control: NIST NCCoE ten tenets (Oct 27 2026, Booth/Fisher/Galluzzo/Clancy) — distinct verifiable agent identity, no idle access, short-lived task-scoped permissions, policy separated from reasoning, continuous monitoring
  • confidential computing: TEEs + attestation protect data in use (CoreWeave Zero Trust AI Framework Oct 21 2026, Fortanix Confidential Containers); honest limit — attestation proves where code ran, not whether the data flow was wise
  • try this: one-page data-flow map + cross-user retrieval test + grep logs/traces for a real email or token from a test run

title: Episode 12 - The Trace Is the Truth
summary: The observability, logging, and tracing deep dive promised in Episode 11: why one trace per task is the artifact that lets you debug, evaluate, and defend an agent, how OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions work in practice in 2026, why coding agents emit three dialects instead of one standard, and where telemetry stops and evals, guardrails, and cost control begin.
description_html:
The observability, logging, and tracing deep dive promised in Episode 11: why one trace per task is the artifact that lets you debug, evaluate, and defend an agent, how OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions work in practice in 2026, why coding agents emit three dialects instead of one standard, and where telemetry stops and evals, guardrails, and cost control begin.

Highlights

  • one trace per task: invoke_agent on top, chat and execute_tool beneath, subagents nested — the tree is the debugger, the eval input, and the audit trail
  • OTel GenAI conventions, June 2026 update: semconv v1.42.0 moved gen_ai.* into a dedicated repo — organisational, not stable; still Development status, no 1.0; pin versions and keep attribute names in one mapping file
  • MCP conventions in the same repo: MCP tool calls trace the same as native tools; content attributes opt-in and off by default (OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT)
  • backend ingestion reality: OTLP makes the backend config, but mapping layers differ — Phoenix converts gen_ai.* since 15.10, Langfuse OTLP HTTP-only with langfuse.* precedence, Datadog native GenAI from v1.37
  • coding-agent dialect problem: Copilot native OTel, Claude Code/Codex hook-based; Jaeger shows three dialects — Claude Code's own attribute names, Codex tokens on the wrong span, Qwen Code faithful but logging prompts by default; hooks are telemetry, not enforcement; CLAUDE.md/skills not captured
  • where OTel stops: no quality judgment, no safety scoring, no enforcement, no cost beyond tokens — evals, guardrails, and cost-per-successful-task are separate layers; monitor the system path, evaluate the answer
  • minimum useful trace: task + authorising actor, tools visible vs called, inputs/outputs redacted at the boundary, approvals/denials/timeouts, tokens/latency/retries/cache/cost, final verifier result; governance fields yours to add, emitted from the harness
  • production mechanics: tail-based sampling (100% of errors/cost outliers, 5–10% of rest); backfill impossible; LangChain 2026 survey — 89% have some observability, only 62% detailed step/tool tracing; token spike as reliability signal
  • try this: pick a past failure and instrument for the 2-minute trace, then point a coding agent at a neutral backend and check tokens/tool spans/model names actually appear

title: Episode 13 - The Gate That Gets Tired
summary: The human-in-the-loop deep dive promised in Episode 12: Anthropic measured it — Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts, so the gate is a reflex, not a check; why approval fatigue and automation bias wear the human out, how Claude Code's auto-mode classifier and six permission modes replace prompts with boundaries, the four oversight patterns, durable pauses and digest-bound approvals, and turning every denial into training data for your next boundary.
description_html:
The human-in-the-loop deep dive promised in Episode 12: Anthropic measured it — Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts, so the gate is a reflex, not a check; why approval fatigue and automation bias wear the human out, how Claude Code's auto-mode classifier and six permission modes replace prompts with boundaries, the four oversight patterns, durable pauses and digest-bound approvals, and turning every denial into training data for your next boundary.

Highlights

  • Anthropic's March 2026 number: Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts — a prompt approved 93% of the time stops being a safety check and turns into a reflex; auto-approve use grows from ~20% of sessions for new users to over 40% at 750 sessions
  • automation bias and oversight saturation: Parasuraman & Manzey (2010); Dratsch et al. 2023 Radiology — inexperienced radiologists' accuracy fell from 79.7% to 19.8% when the AI suggestion was wrong; Mitchell, Ghosh & Passi (2026) — “oversight degrades the overseer”; Gradient Institute oversight saturation (Aug 2026); NIST Tenet 05 consent fatigue (Oct 27, 2026)
  • Claude Code auto mode: transcript classifier on Sonnet 4.6, two-stage (single-token filter, then chain-of-thought); 0.4% false positive rate on real traffic but 17% false negative rate on 52 real overeager actions; escalation at 3 consecutive or 20 total denials; default on all plans from v2.1.283
  • six permission modes — default/Manual, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions — with allow/ask/deny rules (deny first, first match wins); sandboxing cut prompts 84% in internal use
  • four oversight patterns: log only, approve before commit, sampled review after the fact, escalate on trigger — pick by reversibility and blast radius; sampled post-hoc review is the underused one
  • durable pauses: LangGraph interrupt() + checkpointer (no limit), OpenAI Agents SDK needs_approval + RunState, Claude Agent SDK canUseTool (30 days on disk), Bedrock Agents requireConfirmation (90 minutes max); persistent checkpointer, node re-runs from start on resume, gate downstream of the action is a confirmation receipt, approvals bound to the plan digest
  • MCP MRTR (July 2026 spec): input_required + requestState, digest-bound single-use approval, exactly-once execution; preview/execute split for destructive tools
  • approvals as training data: Anthropic's n=52 overeager set was curated from denied/flagged sessions; mine denials for deny rules, 100%-approved prompts for allow policy; EU AI Act Art. 14 (Dec 2, 2027), OWASP LLM06, Gartner 40% cancellation forecast
  • try this: audit your last 50 approval prompts and compute approval rate and median latency — above 90% or under 2 seconds means redesign; split one irreversible tool into preview/execute with a durable, digest-bound interrupt
